To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the high doses of a halotolerent indigenous-gut L. plantarurn reduced the abundance of other commensal lactobacilli without increasing its own abundance in the gut and that this was achieved without causing transintestinal translocations, clinical disease, or other adverse effects.
high doses of halotolearant Lactobacillis plantarum reduce the number of lactobacilli and slightly reduce weight gain in newborn calves.
high oral doses of the halotolerant L. plantarium strain of bovine-origin reduced the fecal abundance of other lactobacillus species without increasing its species abundance in newborn calves.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of a high dose of a halotolerent L. plantarium strain on other gut commensals in newborn calves.
the ecological effects of high doses of halotolerance in newborn calves.
the ecological effect of a probiotic strain on the commensal gut microbiota in newborn calves.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the halotolerance trait in probiotics may have an important role to play in the future selection of probiotic products for use in the human population.

the high doses of the strain L. plantarummay reduce the abundance of lactobacilli without changing the species abundance, causing transient transintestinal translocation of L. plantarium and inducing no clinical signs of disease.

the use of high concentrations of L. plantarm in newborn calves may be beneficial for the reduction of lactobacilli and other commensal bacteria, but not for the reduction of coliforms, and it may have an adverse effect on body weight gain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
high doses of halotolerance is an important characteristic of probiotics that may reduce other commensal lactobacilli.
high doses of halotolarent L. plantarium strain-B80 reduced other commensal lactobacilli without changing its species prevalence in the gut of calves.

the high oral doses of the strain B80 of Lactobacilus plantarum (halotolerant) in newborn calves did not change its species abundance in feces but reduced the number of other lactobacillus species in calves without causing clinical disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
high doses of halotolerance can be a useful selection criterion for probiotic strains.
the use of high oral doses (10-11 CFU) of halotolerants in early life may reduce commensals, and that this effect should be carefully monitored in future studies.
the ecological impact of probiotics on commensals is not always beneficial and that probiotic products should not be assumed to be safe for all individuals.
